extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners, patent practitioners, and applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103, including what prior art may be relied upon, how to determine analogous art, how to compare claimed inventions to the prior art, and how examiners should consider applicant rebuttals and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant’s reply requirements (37 CFR 1.111(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.111(b) requires applicant to distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action. The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable over any applied references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an applicant disagrees with any factual findings by the Office, an effective traverse must include a reasoned statement explaining why the applicant believes the Office has erred substantively as to the factual findings. A mere statement or argument that the Office has not established a prima facie case of obviousness or that the Office’s reliance on common knowledge is unsupported by documentary evidence will not be considered substantively adequate. Office personnel may repeat the rejection made in the prior Office action and make the next Office action final. See MPEP § 706.07(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant’s rebuttal evidence (secondary considerations and unexpected results)
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all rebuttal evidence that is timely presented by the applicants when reevaluating any obviousness determination. Rebuttal evidence may include evidence of 'secondary considerations,' such as 'commercial success, long felt but unsolved needs, [and] failure of others' and may also include evidence of unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once applicant has presented rebuttal evidence, Office personnel should reconsider any initial obviousness determination in view of the entire record. All rejections of record and proposed rejections and their bases should be reviewed to confirm continued viability. The Office action should clearly communicate findings and conclusions and articulate how conclusions are supported by the findings. Follow MPEP § 706.07(a) for finality procedures. See MPEP § 2145 and MPEP § 716 to § 716.10 regarding affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 for traversing grounds of rejection. Case law: In re Piasecki; In re Eli Lilly & Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art availability: 35 U.S.C. 102 prior art may be used for 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: Before answering Graham’s 'content' inquiry, it must be known whether a patent or publication is in the prior art under 35 U.S.C. § 102. Subject matter that is prior art under 35 U.S.C. § 102 can be used to support a rejection under section 103. Admitted prior art can be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations, regardless of whether the admitted prior art would otherwise qualify as prior art under statutory categories of 35 U.S.C. 102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection is based on various 102 categories (e.g., 102(a)(1)/(a)(2) or pre-AIA 102(a),(b),(e)). Examples: an issued U.S. patent more than 1 year before filing can serve as a statutory bar; publications that could be applied under pre-AIA 102(a) may be overcome by affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.131. See MPEP §§ 901, 2121-2129, 2151-2155 for overview of prior art and admissions as prior art (MPEP § 2129).

rubrics_metrics.name: Content of the prior art must be determined as of the time the invention was made (avoid hindsight)
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of the prior art is determined at the time the invention was made to avoid impermissible hindsight. Decisionmakers must 'cast the mind back to the time the invention was made... to occupy the mind of one skilled in the art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement helps avoid hindsight bias when comparing prior art to claimed inventions. See MPEP § 2145 subsection X.A. and W.L. Gore & Associates v. Garlock. Examiners should not rely on later-acquired understanding to judge what would have been obvious at the relevant time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — applicant burden to show conditions apply
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 who wants to avail of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) benefits has the burden of establishing that subject matter which only qualifies as prior art under subsection (e), (f) or (g) of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 used in a rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish joint research provisions of pre-AIA 103(c) (for applications pending on or after Dec 10, 2004), the applicant must establish: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the invention date; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of that agreement; and (C) the patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the agreement. See MPEP § 706.02(l)(1)-(2) and case law (e.g., In re Bartfeld).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference must be analogous prior art to be relied on under 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: In order for a reference to be proper for use in an obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference must be analogous art to the claimed invention. A reference is analogous art if: (1) the reference is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if it addresses a different problem); or (2) the reference is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if it is not in the same field).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must determine what is 'analogous prior art' for obviousness analysis (In re Bigio; KSR v. Teleflex). The examiner may include a statement of the examiner's understanding of the problem to support that a reference is reasonably pertinent. The question often turns on how the problem to be solved is perceived; if an overly narrow view inconsistent with the specification is used, art may be inappropriately limited. Any applicant argument that the examiner misconstrued the problem should be fully considered in light of the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonably pertinent standard — 'logically have commended itself' to an inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: To be 'reasonably pertinent' to the problem, a reference must 'logically [] have commended itself to an inventor's attention in considering his problem.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining if a non-field reference is reasonably pertinent, an examiner should consider the problem faced by the inventor as reflected in the specification and explain factual reasons why the prior art is pertinent (In re ICON Health and Fitness; In re Clay; In re Klein). The examiner should explain why an inventor seeking to solve the identified problem would have looked to the reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider similarities and differences in structure and function (weight over classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: While Patent Office classification and cross-references are some evidence of nonanalogy or analogy, courts have found that similarities and differences in structure and function of the inventions carry far greater weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should focus on structural similarities and functional overlap when assessing whether prior art is pertinent; classification alone is less important. See In re Ellis for an example where structural/functional similarity controlled the analogy determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy in the chemical arts (apply analogous-art test contextually)
rubrics_metrics.description: In chemical arts, teachings across related chemical/carrier/dye arts may be pertinent because solutions in one chemical area would be looked to for similar problems in another; references concerned with absorbing biologically active materials on carriers were pertinent across related problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples (Ex parte Bland; Stratoflex; In re Mlot-Fijalkowski) to justify reliance on references from related chemical or formulation arts when the problem is chemical in nature. Show that the problem to be solved is one of chemistry generally so a search would include those arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy in the mechanical arts (broad exploration of prior art is reasonable)
rubrics_metrics.description: In simple mechanical inventions a broad spectrum of prior art must be explored and it is reasonable to permit inquiry into other areas where one of ordinary skill would be aware similar problems exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court decisions (e.g., Stevenson v. ITC; In re Bigio; In re Deminski) support looking to structurally/functionally similar devices (e.g., toothbrushes for hair brush claims, pumps vs compressors) when the problems and functions overlap. Examiner should consider whether cited prior art shares function/structure with claimed device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy in the electrical arts (look to solutions for similar engineering problems)
rubrics_metrics.description: In electrical/power/control arts, a designer facing a similar engineering problem would look to solutions used in other electrical contexts (e.g., rate-limiting problems across devices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Medtronic v. Cardiac Pacemakers — circuits used to inhibit runaway pulses in high-power/high-frequency devices were pertinent to pacemaker rate-limiting problems. Examiner should assess whether the technical problem is analogous across electrical applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy in the design arts (consider designer's knowledge scope and general use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design references are analogous if they reasonably fall within the scope of knowledge of a designer of ordinary skill and if a prior design has the same general use as that claimed in the design patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 1504.03 and examples (In re Rosen; Ex parte Pappas; In re Butera) — design references from related product categories may be analogous when designers would be aware of those references; but a design for a metal ball anode was nonanalogous to a combined insect repellent and air freshener because designers would not look to an anode design for that combined use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between prior art and claimed invention — consider claimed invention 'as a whole'
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims requires interpreting the claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art references as a whole. The question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is not whether the differences themselves would have been obvious, but whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claims per MPEP §§ 2111-2116.01 and consider all claim limitations. Case examples: Stratoflex v. Aeroquip; Schenck v. Nortron; In re Hirao — admitted unobvious aspects of some claim elements can make the subject matter as a whole nonobvious. Do not improperly focus on a single structural difference to the exclusion of other claim elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not distill invention to a 'gist' or 'thrust'—avoid disregarding 'as a whole' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Distilling an invention down to the 'gist' or 'thrust' disregards the requirement of analyzing the subject matter 'as a whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricting consideration to one perceived advantage or a subset of claim limitations can lead to improper obviousness conclusions. Examples: W.L. Gore; Bausch & Lomb v. Barnes-Hind/Hydrocurve; Jones v. Hardy; Panduit — courts reversed analyses that treated claims as though they read differently than allowed or that treated the advantage as the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of source/cause of problem can be part of 'as a whole' inquiry (may support patentability)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentable invention may lie in the discovery of the source of a problem even though the remedy may be obvious once the source is identified; discovery of the source is part of the 'subject matter as a whole' inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination is fact-specific: discovering the cause of a problem can render the claimed subject matter nonobvious if prior art did not teach that cause or suggest the selection of claim elements (In re Sponnoble). But if prior art contains the same solution for a similar problem, discovery of cause may not result in patentability (In re Wiseman). Use examples (Sponnoble; Wiseman) to support examiner reasoning.
